woven: [AC9S9I06]
unit: equations
title: Where does the mass go?
summary: "In a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, not made or destroyed, so the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. In a closed system the mass reading stays the same. In an open system it can seem to change because a gas escapes (mass falls) or a gas from the air joins in (mass rises); counting the gas shows the mass is still conserved."
language: science
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
hook: "Burn a pile of steel wool and it gets heavier. Burn a log and it gets lighter. Is mass appearing and vanishing?"
---
You can balance an equation, so now you'll work out what a balanced equation tells you about mass. There's no simulation this time, just questions.

## Engage: the fizzing flask

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students see a falling mass reading in an open vessel as mass being destroyed. The mass is in the gas that escaped."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "An antacid tablet is dropped into water in an open beaker on a balance. It fizzes and the balance reading falls. Where has the missing mass gone?"
  options: ["Into the carbon dioxide gas that escaped into the air", "It was destroyed in the reaction", "It turned into energy", "The balance is faulty"]
  actual: "Into the carbon dioxide gas that escaped. If the same reaction were done in a sealed flask, the reading wouldn't change. The mass is conserved: the gas just left the balance."
```

## Explain: counting everything

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Closed-system results, open-system corrections and the link to the balanced equation meet the three success criteria."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why is the total mass the same before and after a reaction in a sealed flask?"
      options: ["Atoms are only rearranged: none are made or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same", "Any gas made has no mass, so only the solids and liquids count", "The flask absorbs the difference"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Gases have mass too. In a sealed flask they stay on the balance, so the reading holds.", "Nothing absorbs mass."]
      explain: "The same atoms are present before and after, just joined in new ways. Same atoms, same total mass."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "In a sealed flask, 12.0 g of magnesium reacts with 8.0 g of oxygen. What mass of magnesium oxide forms (g)?"
      answer: 20
      explain: "The total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants: 12.0 + 8.0 = 20.0 g."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "In an open dish, 2.4 g of magnesium burns and the white ash weighs 4.0 g. What mass of oxygen from the air joined in (g)?"
      answer: 1.6
      explain: "4.0 − 2.4 = 1.6 g. The ash is heavier because it contains oxygen from the air."
    hint: ["What in the air could have joined the magnesium while it burned?", "Everything in the ash is either the magnesium you started with or what joined it, so compare the two masses."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A log burns in an open fire and the ash is much lighter than the log. Is mass conserved?"
      options: ["Yes: most of the mass left as carbon dioxide and water vapour, which spread into the air", "No: burning destroys mass", "Yes: because the ash is the same thing as the log"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Mass isn't destroyed: it left as gases.", "Ash is a different substance from wood."]
      explain: "Count the gases, and the total mass of reactants (wood and oxygen) equals the total mass of products (ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour)."
    hint: "What are the products when wood burns, and which of them are still sitting in the fireplace?"
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "The balanced equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms on each side. What does this tell you about mass?"
      options: ["The same atoms are on each side, so the mass is the same before and after", "Water is lighter than hydrogen and oxygen together", "Nothing: equations don't show mass"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Water has the same mass as the hydrogen and oxygen that make it.", "A balanced equation is a record of the atoms, and so of the mass."]
      explain: "Balancing is the same idea as conservation of mass: each atom appears on both sides the same number of times."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can explain why mass is conserved in a reaction and why it can seem to change in an open system." }
```

## Elaborate: predict the products

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Using conservation to predict a mass of product from the mass of reactants shows the principle as a tool."
check:
  type: number
  q: "Iron (5.6 g) reacts completely with sulfur (3.2 g) in a sealed tube to make iron sulfide. What mass of iron sulfide forms (g)?"
  answer: 8.8
  explain: "5.6 + 3.2 = 8.8 g."
```

## Elaborate: waste

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Mass is always conserved, but not all of it is the product you want; this is what green chemistry tries to improve."
check:
  type: question
  q: "If mass is always conserved, why do chemists worry about waste?"
  options: ["The atoms that end up in unwanted by-products are wasted for the purpose, even though they still exist", "Mass can be destroyed in a factory", "Waste is only a problem for the environment"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "It can't be: that is the point of the law.", "It is also a cost and resource problem."]
  explain: "Conservation says nothing is lost, but atoms in by-products aren't in the product you wanted. Good reactions put more of the atoms into the product."
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the fizzing beaker with what conservation of mass says." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- In a chemical reaction atoms are **rearranged, not made or destroyed**, so the total mass is **conserved**.
- In a **closed system** the mass stays the same.
- In an **open system** it can seem to change because a **gas escapes** or **joins in from the air**; counting the gas shows the mass is still conserved.
- A **balanced equation** has the same atoms on both sides.

```teacher
summary: Students explain why total mass is conserved in a closed reaction,
  account for apparent changes in open systems, and connect balanced equations
  to mass conservation (AC9S9U07, node 5, an integration node).
time: 15
timing: Engage 3 min · Explain 9 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical adds 1 min,
  Wider about 1 min
goals:
  - I can explain why mass is conserved in a closed system.
  - I can explain why mass seems to change in an open system.
  - I can say what a balanced equation shows about mass.
before: >
  A short questions-led lesson with no simulation, after Balancing equations.
  Set the width with `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or `wider`. It works
  best paired with a real investigation: weigh an antacid tablet and water in an
  open beaker, then in a sealed zip-lock bag.


  The numbers in the questions are chosen for clean answers: magnesium and
  oxygen combine in a ratio of 3 to 2 by mass, and iron and sulfur react in a
  ratio of about 7 to 4.
running:
  - "Engage: tally the predictions. Ask the 'destroyed' group where the carbon
    dioxide went."
  - "Explain: the closed-system sum and the open-system case are the success
    criteria."
  - "In your own words: why the reading dropped and what to change."
struggle: Counting all the substances, including gases. When a student says mass
  was lost, ask what else was in the system that they didn't weigh.
stuck:
  - see: A student says burning destroys the wood.
    ask: What are the products of burning wood?
    fix: Carbon dioxide and water vapour (gases) and ash. Their mass adds up to the
      wood plus the oxygen used.
  - see: A student says mass appears when magnesium burns.
    ask: What in the air could join the magnesium?
    fix: Oxygen. The product is heavier because it has oxygen in it.
stretch: "6.0 g of carbon burns completely in 16.0 g of oxygen. What mass of
  carbon dioxide forms? (22.0 g.) What mass would be left of the oxygen if only
  12.0 g was available? (Not enough: the product would be less than 22.0 g.)"
support: "Give a sentence frame: 'The balance reading went (up / down) because
  ___ (entered / left) the container. The total mass of everything is still
  ___.'"
leads: >
  Next: Year 10 atoms and the periodic table.


  In class: antacid tablet and water in an open beaker and in a sealed zip-lock
  bag on a balance; steel wool on a balance with a flame; vinegar and baking
  soda in a bottle with a balloon.
exit:
  q: A student weighs a candle before and after burning it in an open dish and
    finds it lighter. Is mass conserved?
  a: Yes. The missing mass left as carbon dioxide and water vapour. Weighing the
    candle and the oxygen used against the gases would show the same total.
explain: >
  Atoms are **rearranged**, not made or destroyed, so total mass is
  **conserved**. In an **open system** the mass can seem to change when a gas
  escapes or enters. A **balanced equation** has the same atoms on both sides.
```
